title: Studio film work and film stars
summary: The house band was called to studios for sound pictures at $10 an hour; he recalls Sylvia Sidney, Mae West and obbligato for My Old Flame.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: And they had where -- a steady house band there.

Oh yes. They were very big because in those days movies was very -- a very big thing, and I believe that there were very few weeks that we didn't have two or three days out at the studios. And the studios were very -- were top things in the business at that time.

Musically it was -- it paid so well. IN fact, the pay at that time was $10.00 an hour in the studios. And your day started at 9:00 in the morning, and ended at 4:00. And the music was recorded along with the sound and the picture --
the camera work, so we had to sit there very quietly, or play with things that would fit with the volume, and oh, it was just everything. It was all done together.
The dialogue and the music was all done together?

Yeah, all done at the same time. They would be speaking over there, and when your turn came to play you would play, and you'd quiet down -- like if it was a dance scene on the floor you'd quiet down so that you didn't cover up the voices of the actors. And oh, it was terrific. And so you see we -- the time stretched out quite a bit and you made a whole lot of money.
But every time there was a retake, you'd do the music too.
You'd take some day -- sometimes it would take all morning to take one scene. And a lot of times you was just sitting there, waiting for your time. You see, it was nothing like it is today.
What studios did you work at?
Oh, practically all of them. I remember Metro Goldwyn Mayer. It was -- oh mostly all the studios.
There was an
RKO Pathe, wasn't it?
RKO -- everything. Every studio.
Do you remember the names of the studios during that era? I know that a lot of them are

different than now -- Well, I don't recall too much of them. I remember that practically all of them -- they were -- it was such big business. They even had studio orchestras, which they don't have anymore. And the studio hired their own orchestras. And -- oh, it was terrific. It was very good.
Do you remember any specific films that you played on?
Ah --
Or any stars that you worked with?
(PAUSE)
Oh, oneof our 7- one of our first actresses I remember was Sylvia Sidney. And the -- in fact we worked so many of them that I can't keep track of the stars. Mae West and oh, all of them.

The reason I'm asking specifically is because I think it would be very interesting to see an old film made during that era right now -- maybe on television -- and hear the trombone and realize that that is Lawrence Brown playing on that film score, which most people don't know. That's why I was wondering if you could remember any of the films --

Well, this was later on in the career when we played behind Mae West. I remember I did the obligato background to 'My Old Flame.' With Mae West in the picture. I think that's about the only time I ever did that. And then
I worked with other orchestras in pictures -- just gangs and gangs of them.
During what years did you do the film work? this one?
Well, that was from '27 on. See I worked with so many different people that it's right now --
